title: Sound Illusions
sub: When Your Ears Deceive You · Grades 5–8 · Music · 30 minutes
objective: Students will experience auditory illusions firsthand, analyze how music and sound manipulate emotions, and connect sound deception to visual deception explored in the Mini Museum exhibition.
materials: Audio clips: Shepard Tone, McGurk Effect video, Yanny/Laurel clip
Two versions of same scene with different music (happy vs. scary)
Speakers or headphones for clear audio playback
Optional: Mini Museum stereoscope for visual/audio comparison
connection: **Option 1 — Visit:** The stereoscope creates a 3D illusion for the eyes, just as binaural audio creates spatial illusions for the ears. Spirit photography manipulated visual trust; film scores manipulate emotional trust.

steps.title: The Endless Staircase of Sound
script: Play the Shepard Tone (an auditory illusion that seems to rise forever).

*“Listen to this sound. What do you notice? Does it seem to go up… and up… and up? But here’s the trick — it’s actually looping. Your ears are being fooled, just like your eyes can be fooled by optical illusions. Today we’re going to explore how sound can deceive us.”*

screen.question: Listen to this sound. What do you notice? Does it seem to go up… and up… and up?

steps.purpose: Ears can be fooled just as eyes can.

steps.title: Yanny or Laurel?
script: **Illusion 1: Yanny or Laurel?** Play the famous clip. Have students vote. Reveal that the same sound can be heard differently based on which frequencies your brain focuses on.
steps.purpose: One clip, two answers: the brain decides what it hears.

steps.title: McGurk Effect
script: **Illusion 2: McGurk Effect** (if video available). Show how what we SEE changes what we HEAR — demonstrating that our senses work together and can be fooled together.
*“Your brain doesn’t just passively receive sound — it actively interprets it. And that interpretation can be manipulated.”*

screen.question: Your brain doesn’t just passively receive sound — it actively interprets it.

steps.purpose: What we see changes what we hear.

steps.title: Same scene, different music
script: Show the same neutral video clip twice with different background music:
*“How did the music change what you felt about this scene? The visuals were identical — only the sound changed. Filmmakers, advertisers, and game designers use this technique constantly.”*

screen.question: How did the music change what you felt about this scene?

steps.purpose: The visuals stay the same; only the sound changes.

steps.title: Discuss
script: **Discuss:** How do horror movies use sound? How do commercials use music? How do video games use audio cues?

screen.question: How do horror movies use sound? How do commercials use music? How do video games use audio cues?

steps.purpose: Find the same technique in films, ads and games.

steps.title: Musical elements of manipulation
script: Quick analysis of HOW music manipulates:
**Instrumentation:** Strings = emotion; Brass = power; Synth = futuristic/unsettling
*“Once you know these tricks, you can recognize when someone is trying to manipulate your emotions through sound — and you can make conscious choices about how to respond.”*

cells: Strings = emotion; Brass = power; Synth = futuristic/unsettling

steps.purpose: Four elements to listen for, so students can recognize them.
students: Which did you hear in the clip?

steps.title: The Aware Listener
script: *“Just like the Mini Museum shows us that our eyes can be tricked by photographs and illusions, today we learned that our ears can be tricked too. The Victorians were fooled by spirit photographs because the technology was new. We can be fooled by sound design because we don’t always notice it. But now you know — and knowing is the first step to not being manipulated.”*

screen.question: But now you know — and knowing is the first step to not being manipulated.

steps.purpose: Ears, like eyes, can be tricked; knowing is the first defence.
students: Name one way you’ll listen more critically to music in media this week.
